opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because for a long time our approach was mostly to be the model layer and let partners build the products on top. And we still love that. A lot of the best coding tools out there are built on Claude, and we want that ecosystem to thrive.

But a couple of things pushed us toward building something ourselves. The first is that coding has become one of the clearest places where these models deliver real, measurable value. People were using Claude to write and refactor code, debug, and navigate big codebases. We felt we needed to be close to that experience firsthand. When you're the one shipping the product, you feel every rough edge. You see where the model gets confused, where it's overconfident, where it needs better tools. That feedback loop is incredibly valuable for making the models better, and it's hard to get secondhand.

The second is that we wanted to explore what a more agentic form factor looks like. Autocomplete in an editor is one thing. Giving the model a terminal, letting it read files, run tests, and iterate on its own work is a pretty different paradigm. We wanted to push on that frontier and figure out the right interaction patterns: how much autonomy to give it, when it should check in with you, how you keep the human in control. Those are questions we care about from a safety perspective too, not just a product perspective. Agents acting in real environments are where a lot of the interesting alignment challenges show up.

Honestly, part of it was also just that our own engineers wanted it. People internally started using early versions and got hooked, and that's usually a good sign you're onto something. So it felt like the right move: learn directly, set a bar for what agentic coding can look like, and feed everything we learn back into the models that everyone, including our partners, gets to use.

r001.rationale: It says coding is a clear area where Claude models deliver measurable value and that this motivated Anthropic to build and learn from its own coding product.

r002.rationale: It says shipping the product firsthand reveals rough edges and provides a valuable feedback loop that is hard to get secondhand from partners.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started as an internal tool. We weren't planning a product. Boris Cherny built this little terminal thing so he could point Claude at our own codebase and have it actually do things, run the tests, edit files, poke around the repo, instead of copy-pasting snippets back and forth from a chat window. And within a few weeks, something like three-quarters of the company's engineers were using it every day. That's the signal you can't ignore. When your own people voluntarily switch their workflow overnight, you've found something real.

The deeper reason, though, is that we felt a gap between what the model could do and what people were actually experiencing. We had this model that was genuinely capable of agentic work, of taking a vague goal and grinding through it across many steps, and the dominant interfaces at the time were autocomplete or chat. Those are fine, but they put the human in the loop at every keystroke. They hide most of the model's capability. We wanted people to feel what it's like when the model is a collaborator that goes off and does the task, not a fancy typeahead.

And there's a strategic piece too. Coding is where frontier capability shows up first. Developers are the most demanding users, they notice every regression, and they'll tell you instantly when something's wrong. Owning that surface directly means we learn faster than if we only ever saw the model through someone else's product. That feedback loop goes straight back into how we train the next model.

It also fit Anthropic's safety mission, which people find surprising. If you believe these systems are going to be doing more and more autonomous work, you want to be the ones figuring out what permission models look like, what it means to let an agent run a command, how much a human should review. Better to learn those lessons in the open with developers who understand the tradeoffs than to have them learned for us later in some higher-stakes setting.

So the short version is: our engineers wouldn't put it down, the market hadn't built the thing yet, and we thought the fastest way to show what the model could really do was to just ship it.

r001.rationale: The response says Anthropic’s model could handle agentic coding work, while existing interfaces hid much of that capability, and that shipping Claude Code would let users experience it directly.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says owning the coding surface directly lets Anthropic learn faster than seeing the model only through someone else’s product.

astra-6.text:
We were seeing how much people wanted to use Claude for coding, but there was still a lot of friction. You’d copy code into a chat window, get a suggestion, paste it back, run it, and then bring the error back to Claude. The model could help with individual steps, but the human was doing all the coordination.

Claude Code was a way to close that loop. Give Claude access to the codebase and the ability to make changes and run tests, and you can delegate a task rather than shuttle text back and forth.

And building that experience ourselves gives us a much tighter feedback loop. We learn where the model is useful, where it gets stuck, and what people need to feel comfortable trusting it with more work. That informs both the product and the next generation of models.

r001.rationale: The response describes coding demand and the friction Claude Code addresses, but it does not identify Anthropic’s coding-model capabilities as an advantage or reason for building the application.

r002.rationale: It says building the product provides a tighter feedback loop and helps Anthropic learn from users, but it does not compare this with relying on partners or state that the direct relationship enables faster learning.

sol-6.1.text:
We were seeing this gap between what the model could do and what people could actually get out of it. You could ask Claude a coding question, but then you were copying code back and forth, running it yourself, and bringing the errors back. The model was increasingly capable of doing that whole loop.

So Claude Code was a way to put Claude where developers already work and let it read the codebase, make changes, run tests, and iterate. Building that experience directly also gives us a much tighter feedback loop. We learn where the model gets stuck, where it needs better tools, and when it should ask the user for help. That informs both the product and the next generation of models.

r001.rationale: It says Claude was increasingly capable of handling the full coding loop, which motivated building Claude Code to let developers use that capability directly.

r002.rationale: It describes a tighter feedback loop from building the product directly, but does not say Anthropic learns faster than it would through partners.
